87	## The glyphs of no width
88	
89	The curator's note of 2026-11-16: on his phone the table of section E.2.3 of Appendix E showed `=` in the row "`=/=` becomes ≠", where the PDF shows ≠ (`curator-notes.md`).
90	
91	- **The cause.** TeX has no glyph for ≠. It sets the slash of `\not` (code 54 of the symbol font cmsy), a glyph whose width is zero and whose ink lies to the right of its place, and then `=` over it. The bar of `\mapsto` (code 55) is the same kind, set before →. dvisvgm writes each as a character whose advance is zero. The slash and `=` are in different fonts (cmsy and cmr), so the slash came out alone: `<text class='t2' x='80.33' y='56.19'></text>`, a piece of text of no width. Nothing was lost in the conversion: the LaTeX, the DVI, the SVG and the font piece all held the slash, and Chromium painted it. The phone's browser did not paint that piece of text. The bar of ↦, which stands in one `<text>` with its arrow, was painted there.
92	- **Not shown here.** No browser but Chromium runs in the container (Playwright's WebKit lacks its system libraries), so the phone's picture was not reproduced, and which rule of its browser drops the piece is not established; the reading above rests on his report, on the SVG, and on the difference between the slash (alone, lost) and the bar (with its arrow, kept).
93	- **The repair** (`draw_widthless` in `spec2html.py`). After the fonts are read, every character whose glyph has an advance of zero is taken out of the text of every display, and the glyph's outline, read from the same font piece, is drawn at its place as `<path class='nw'>`. Nothing else moves, since the glyph had no advance. This covers the slash alone, the slash beside its sign and the bar: 161 glyphs in the Working Draft and 177 in the revised edition, on 20 pages of each. The build fails if a display still leaves such a glyph to the text. In Chromium the displays look as before.
94	- **The places.** `widthless-glyphs-2026-11-16.md` lists them by page and section. The lost kind, the slash alone, stood at 68 places of the Working Draft and 84 of the revised edition, each showing its sign without the slash (`=` for ≠ at 45 and 55 of them). The worst: section 33.1, Rational Numbers (25 in the Working Draft); sections I.1.11 to I.1.13 and I.1.25 of Appendix I in the revised edition (42); section 41.1 (9 in each); the rules of the calculi in sections A.2.2, A.3.3 and A.4.3 (12 in each), where a premise read `=` for ≠.
95	- **Inside a sentence** a formula is HTML text, and the converter writes ≠, ∉ and their like as one Unicode character, so nothing of this kind is there. Where Unicode has no character for a negated sign, the converter writes the sign and U+0338, the combining slash, which the device's font draws: 25 places in each edition, most in chapter 34 (⊏, ⊐, ⊒, ≣ and others). They were not changed. One was wrong for another reason and is repaired: `S \not\excludes D` in the proof of overloading resolution showed the word "mathrel" with a slash, because the tree's macro `\excludes` is `\mathrel{\lozenge}`; it now shows ◊ with the slash.
96	- **The walk-through of microGPT** (`explorations/microgpt-walk/notation.py`) makes its SVGs by the same method. Its pages use no glyph of no width; its build now reports one as a problem.
97	
98	## The edition's layer over the authors' text
99	
100	This layer is the revised edition's only; the Working Draft has none of it. The source text is not changed for any of this; the converter adds it, and it is visible as the edition's.
101	
102	- **The tint.** What the 2026 revival added stands on a light tint of the ground (`.rv` and `aside.revision` in `reader.css`, the colour `--rev-bg`, in light and in dark): the callout of a revised passage, the revival's paragraph in the preface, the revival's section of Appendix I, and the links below. The contents page and the preface open with one sentence that shows the tint and says what it means. The converter knows the revival's paragraph and section from two short lists at its top, `REVIVAL_PARAGRAPHS` and `REVIVAL_SECTIONS`: the source does not mark them.
103	- **Archived copies.** Beside each address of the authors' text (`http://projectfortress.sun.com` and the others, also in the references), the edition puts a link "archived copy" to `https://web.archive.org/web/2008/<address>`. The Internet Archive resolves a partial date to the nearest capture. 2008 is the year of the release that the preface names with the address; `ARCHIVE` at the top of the script sets it. The container cannot reach the Internet Archive, so no link was opened.
104	- Not built, because the curator has not decided it: marking which words of a revised passage changed (`curator-notes.md`, "The revival's callouts do not show which text changed").
105	
106	## The reader
107	
108	- **Place.** A chapter page stores, in `localStorage` under `fortress-spec.place.v1` (the Working Draft) or `fortress-spec-revival.place.v1` (the revised edition), the block at the top of the screen, for each chapter and for the last one read. The start page offers to continue there; a chapter opened from the contents offers the place where that chapter was left.
109	- **Notes.** The pencil at the end of a paragraph, in the bar of a code example, under a table or beside a heading opens a text box under that place. `notes.html` lists all notes, exports them as text, and imports such a text. They are kept under `fortress-spec.notes.v1`, or `fortress-spec-revival.notes.v1` in the revised edition.
110	- **Without storage** (private browsing) the pages work, a note lasts until the page is left, and a warning says so.
111	- **Select.** The button beside a heading selects that section's text up to its first subsection, for Speak.
112	
113	### The ids that notes hang on
114	
115	- The id of a paragraph is a hash of its words (`#p-934d16e7`). Every paragraph of the first sample keeps its id, among them the two that carry the curator's notes, `preface.html#p-0ea553b6` and `preface.html#p-033235cb`. To keep them, the hash still counts the words "[not converted yet]" after a reference into a chapter outside the first sample, as that sample showed them; the edition's own links are not counted.
116	- One paragraph of chapter 4 changed its id, because its words changed: the one with a quote pair inside a typewriter span (decision 6). 
117	- 2026-11-16: one paragraph changed its id, because its words changed (the repair of `\not\excludes`, above): `overloaded-functional.html#p-e3f30724` became `#p-c3996be5` in the Working Draft, and `spec-changes.html#p-f691a211` became `#p-69abb85a` in the revised edition. None of the curator's notes is on it. The repair of the glyphs of no width changed no id.
118	- The ids of tables (`t-`), grammar boxes (`g-`), and code blocks without a source form (`c-`) changed: 34 in the first sample's chapters (14 in chapter 2, 12 in chapter 4, 2 in chapter 5, 6 in chapter 6). They were hashes of the HTML that the converter's own rendering made, which is gone; they are now hashes of the display's LaTeX source. A code block with a source form keeps its id. `reader.js` keeps a note whose place is gone and lists it at the top of its chapter, with the words it was written on.
119	
120	### The notes across the two editions
121	
122	Notes written before 2026-11-15 were written on the revised edition at the addresses that now show the Working Draft, and they are in the browser under `fortress-spec.notes.v1`. `localStorage` belongs to the host, not to the folder, so both editions can read it.
123	
124	- The Working Draft keeps that key. A paragraph that the revival did not change has the same words, so the same id, in both editions, and its note stays on it.
125	- A note on a block that only the revised edition has (its id is in `revised-only.js`) stays in the Working Draft's storage. Its chapter page lists it at the top with "The passage of this note is in the revised edition" and a link to the passage there; `notes.html` lists it with the same words, and the export gives it the link into `revival/` and a line `Edition: the passage of this note is in the revised edition`. An import reads such a note back.
126	- The revised edition has its own storage. Once, on the first page of it that a browser opens, it takes a copy of the notes of the old key whose passage only it has, so that such a note also shows on its passage; nothing else is copied, and nothing is removed from the old key (`fortress-spec-revival.adopted.v1` records that it was done).
127	- Of the curator's 15 notes of `notes-export-2026-11-15.txt`, 14 stay on their paragraphs of the Working Draft (`preface.html`: `p-0ea553b6`, `p-f85a28b6`, `p-0ee6a8b8`, `p-56c0c623`, `p-3e0c2dfb`; `intro.html`: `p-f9d62312`, `p-284c2aab`, `p-edfaffe1`, `p-a3cd883e`; `overview.html`: `p-136580aa`, `p-18267c77`, `p-ade874e1`, `p-e17a0706`, `p-ffe59943`), and one, on the revival's paragraph of the preface (`p-033235cb`), is listed as a note whose passage is in the revised edition and is copied there. `check.js` imports the file and checks this.
128	
129	## Changes to reader.css and reader.js
130	
131	Of 2026-11-15, for the two editions:
132	
133	- `reader.js`: the storage keys take their prefix from `data-store` on `<body>` (a page without the attribute has `fortress-spec`, as before); `data-edition` on `<body>` is `draft` or `revised`; `window.FORTRESS_REVISED_ONLY`, if a page defines it before `reader.js`, marks the notes whose passage is in the revised edition (their link, a line on their card, a line `Edition:` in the export), and lets the revised edition take its copy once. A page that sets none of the three behaves as before.
134	- `reader.css`, added at its end: `.edline`, `.edline.top` (the edition's own lines), `ol.editions` and `section.apart` (the page of the editions). No rule was changed or removed.
135	
136	Of 2026-11-13:
137	
138	For a page that uses the reader's files, such as the walk-through under `docs/microgpt/`:
139	
140	- `reader.js` is unchanged.
141	- No rule of `reader.css` was changed or removed, and no class was renamed.
142	- Added to `reader.css`, at its end: `svg.tx` and `svg.tx.il` (a display, and one inside a sentence), `.mw` (the frame of a long formula inside a sentence), `.rv`, `a.ed`, `.legend` (the edition's layer), `.doc` (the documentation text of an API listing), `.hr` (a rule inside a formula), and `white-space: normal` for `.m` inside headings, `dt`, `figcaption`, `summary` and `nav`.
143	- The converter no longer writes these, whose rules stay in the stylesheet: `.fx-r .tb`, `.fx-r .l`, `.gapline`, `.cm`, `table.tab`, `table.grammar`, `div.words`, `.tw.gr .label`. `.fx-r`, `.dm` and `.tw` now hold one `svg.tx`.
144	- A chapter page with displays links `tex-fonts.css` and carries a `<style>` with the font classes of its SVGs (`svg.tx text.t0` and so on).
145	
146	## The checks
147	
148	Serve the pages, then run the three:
149	
150	    mkdir -p /tmp/spec-srv && ln -sfn "$PWD/docs" /tmp/spec-srv/fortress
151	    python3 -m http.server 8765 --directory /tmp/spec-srv &
152	    S=explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html U=http://localhost:8765/fortress/specification/
153	    node $S/check.js $U                                   # the Working Draft
154	    node $S/check.js ${U}revival/ /tmp/shots-revised      # the revised edition
155	    node $S/compare.js /tmp/spec-html-work-draft $U
156	    node $S/compare.js /tmp/spec-html-work ${U}revival/
157	    python3 $S/pdfcheck.py                                # the revised edition against Specification/fortress.pdf
158	    git show 414b790e3f:Specification/fortress.pdf > /tmp/spec-html-work-draft/draft-2026-08-21.pdf
159	    python3 $S/pdfcheck.py --pages docs/specification --pdf /tmp/spec-html-work-draft/draft-2026-08-21.pdf
160	
161	The tree holds no PDF of the Working Draft. The nearest is in git: `414b790e3f` (2026-08-21) committed the first PDF that the revival built, before it revised the text; its LaTeX differs from the frozen copy in the preamble of `fortress.tex` (the build's repair) and one line of `basic-lib/objects.tex`, and its library listings are those of the library of that day. `pdfcheck.py` on the Working Draft runs against that file.
162	
163	- **`check.js`** (about a minute) opens every page that the contents lists at 390 px, light and dark. It fails on a page that scrolls sideways, on a construct left unconverted, on a display whose font is missing or lacks a character, on a display that leaves a glyph of no width to the browser's text (it asks the browser for the extent of every character of every display, and a visible character of extent zero fails), and if the ink of the displays is not the colour of the text in both themes. It reads the edition from the page and checks: in the revised edition, `noindex` on every page, the line at the top with its link to the same page of the Working Draft, the two note-carrying ids of the preface, the archive link and the tint; in the Working Draft, no robots tag, no callout, tint, legend or archive link on any page, the link to the revised chapter at the foot and nowhere else, and the curator's 15 notes of 2026-11-15 across the two editions. In both it checks that the text of a display can be selected, the three rules for code inside a sentence, and the curly quote pair. Then, as before: notes on a paragraph, a code example and a heading, the place, export and import, the switch between the two forms of the code, Select, that no request leaves the site, and the pages without `localStorage`. It saves two screenshots.
164	- **`compare.js`** (about five minutes) sets each chapter's displays a second time, with `pdflatex` from the same file, makes a picture of each page with `pdftoppm`, takes a picture of the same display in Chromium, and compares the two: their sizes, and the share of the ink of each that lies within two pixels of the other's. This is the check that would have caught the chapter 4 tables of the first sample. It found two faults while this run was built: dvisvgm wrote the Courier font without the characters U+002E to U+005F when it wrote the whole font at once (the fonts are now written in pieces of 32 codes, and the build reads each piece back and fails if a character that a display uses is missing), and the frame of a table lost its top and left lines at the edge of the picture (each SVG now has a margin). It did not and cannot see the fault of 2026-11-16, the slash of ≠ that a phone did not paint, for two reasons. It looks through Chromium, which painted the slash, so its two pictures agreed. And its measure is the share of a whole display's ink: a trial that hid every glyph of no width in four chapters left all but one display over the limit of 92 %, and the largest connected piece of ink that went missing was 12 to 24 pixels, where displays without a fault differ by pieces of up to 33 pixels (hinting), so no limit on a piece separates the two. `check.js` has the check for this kind.
165	- **`pdfcheck.py`** (ten seconds) reduces every paragraph, heading, list item, caption and display of the pages to its letters and digits, does the same with the text of `Specification/fortress.pdf`, and looks for each block's runs of ten characters in the PDF. A block that lost a row, was set from the wrong source or was filled with something else fails. It found the lemma numbers of Appendix B, the lost footnotes of grammar boxes, and four commands that the text form had mishandled (`\rule`, `\vspace*`, `\not` before a macro, and the calculi's own `\exp`).
166	
167	Results of 2026-11-16, on both editions, after the repair of the glyphs of no width:
168	
169	- `check.js`: all pass on the Working Draft (46 checks) and on the revised edition (43). The new check fails on the pages as they were before the repair (50 characters of no extent on the Working Draft's pages).
170	- `compare.js` (about thirty-five minutes for each edition, both at once, beside other work on the machine): the Working Draft, 1,177 displays compared, 3 differ; the revised edition, 1,229 compared, 4 differ; the same displays as on 2026-11-15, none by a fault of the page.
171	- `pdfcheck.py`: the revised edition, 6,845 blocks, 7 not found; the Working Draft against the PDF of `414b790e3f`, 5,680 blocks, 17 not found. One fewer in each than on 2026-11-15: the paragraph of `\not\excludes`.
172	
173	Results of 2026-11-15, on both editions:
174	
175	- `check.js`: all pass on the Working Draft (45 checks) and on the revised edition (42).
176	- `pdfcheck.py`, the revised edition: 6,845 blocks, 8 not found, as on 2026-11-13. The Working Draft against the PDF of `414b790e3f`: 5,680 blocks, 18 not found: 7 displays of chapter 29, whose listing is the library of February 2011 where that PDF lists the library of August 2026, and 11 blocks at 58–75 % of their runs, dense with symbols or holding a draft note.
177	- `compare.js` (about fifteen minutes for each edition when both run at once): the Working Draft, 1,177 displays compared, 3 differ; the revised edition, 1,229 compared, 4 differ; none by a fault of the page. The three of chapter 16 are those of 2026-11-13, in both editions. The fourth, display 1 of chapter 26 in the revised edition, holds a reference: the second LaTeX run frames it as hyperref frames a link, which makes its picture seven pixels wider.
178	
179	Results of 2026-11-13, on the 54 pages (then one edition, the revised one):
180	
181	- `check.js`: all pass.
182	- `compare.js`: 1,229 displays compared, 5 differ, none by a fault of the page. Three of chapter 16 agree to 77–92 % where the limit is 92 % (one small glyph, and a row of typewriter symbols that the two renderers hint differently). One of chapter 23 holds a citation and one of chapter 33 a reference, which the reader shows as a key and a link and the second LaTeX run shows as `?`.
183	- `pdfcheck.py`: 6,845 blocks compared, 8 not found in the PDF, each with 63–75 % of its runs where the limit is 75 %: three paragraphs and five displays dense with symbols (chapters 9, 13, 16, 40 and Appendix F), read and found right. 98 more are displays of symbols with too few letters to judge by words; `compare.js` covers them.
184	
185	What these checks do not do, and what was looked at by eye:
186	
187	- No tool here places a display beside its page of the PDF. `compare.js` compares with LaTeX's picture from the same source and macros as the PDF, and `pdfcheck.py` compares words with the PDF. Together they cover every display, but neither is a person looking at the PDF's page.
188	- Looked at beside the PDF's page, at 390 px and at a desktop's width: the preface; the character tables of chapter 4 (page 45 of the PDF, the curator's example: the `&`, the row, and the white brackets are right) and its reserved words (page 51); the grammar boxes of sections 7.1 and 9.5 (page 96); Figure 16.1 (page 172); Figure 22.1 (page 228); the first two figures of Appendix A (page 506); sections F.2 to F.4 of Appendix F (page 547).
189	- Not looked at beside the PDF by a person: the other displays and tables, among them most of the 979 rows of the operator tables of Appendix F, the inference rules of Appendix A apart from the first figure, and the API listings.
190	
191	## What differs from the PDF
192	
193	| What | Where | Why |
194	|---|---|---|
195	| A display does not reflow | every chapter | It is LaTeX's page at the PDF's width; on a phone a wide one scrolls inside its frame. |
196	| Formulas inside a sentence are HTML text in the device's fonts | every chapter | The curator's decision. Brackets do not stretch, spacing is the browser's, a fraction is two short lines. |
197	| Some symbols of a display copy as private-use characters | displays with `⟦ ⟧`, `⊢`, primes, large delimiters and other glyphs that the TeX fonts name without a Unicode value | dvisvgm gives such a glyph a code point from U+E000. The picture is right; a copy of the text, and Speak, get a character without meaning. |
198	| The slash of a negated sign and the bar of ↦ are drawings, not text | 161 places of the Working Draft's displays, 177 of the revised edition's | "The glyphs of no width". A copy of ≠ from a display gives `=`; before, it gave a private-use character and `=`. |
199	| The bibliography's numbers | every `\cite`, also inside displays | The PDF numbers the cited works; the reader cites by key, `[JLS]`, and `references.html` lists every entry of `fortress.bib` under its key. |
200	| The index | every `\index` | Dropped; the reader has no index page. |
201	| The arrowheads of the five drawings are solid | chapter 22 | The PDF is made by pdflatex with `eepicemu`, which cannot fill; the reader's drawings come from `latex` with `eepic`, which fills them as the drawing asks. |
202	| Figures and tables stay where their source is | every chapter | None floats to the top of a page. |
203	| A display inside a draft note has the size of the text | a few notes | In the PDF the note's box sets it smaller, in the sans face. |
204	| The API listings show today's library | chapters 29 and 30 | They are made from the `.fsi` files of the tree, as the build makes them; a listing has no source form in the reader. |
205	| The page numbers of `\pageref` | rare | The reader has no pages. |
206	| The title page and the table of contents | front | The contents page of the reader stands for both. |
207	| Appendix I's section of the revival is tinted as a whole | Appendix I | The edition's layer. |
208	
209	The commented source before a hand-written example is the authors' own, and nothing checks that it still matches the LaTeX under it.
210	
211	## Faults of the source text that the conversion met
212	
213	Nothing under `Specification/` was changed. These are for whoever edits it:
214	
215	- `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:17` holds `\tracingcommands=1\tracingmacros=1`, a TeX debugging switch left in the chapter. It prints nothing, but it makes the build's log very large from there on.
216	- `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:45`, in a margin note: ``\b'' is LaTeX's accent command (a bar under the next character), where the authors meant a backslash and the letter b. The PDF shows a quotation mark with a bar under it.
217	- `Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:866`: of three quoted code points in one sentence, the second has its quote pair inside the typewriter span and the others outside (`` `\txt{001C}', \txt{`FBAB'}, `\txt{1D11E}' ``). The reader shows all three alike.

"Walk" is the interpreter. "The compiled path" is `fortress compile` and `fortress run`. Only the compiled path has a static type checker. An "api" is a component's interface file, as a C header is. "Inference" is the checker working out a type that the program did not write. ## The answer - The sentences are not simply wrong. They are a promise of which about half was kept. - The favourable reading is this. A type may be left out wherever something else in the program already states it. The checker copies it from there. The places that can state it are: the api, the declaration that a method implements, the value on the right of `=`, a function's body (for the return type), and the function type that the surrounding code expects. The introduction says "wherever possible", and these are the possible places. - That reading is built for the api, for the right side of `=` (variables, not fields), for return types, and for a function expression. It is shown in the specification's own examples and not built for a method that implements an inherited declaration. It is written in one sentence and not built for a default value of a parameter. - One thing in the specification's examples goes beyond that reading: a top-level function such as `f(x) = x^2 + sin x - cos 2 x`, where nothing but the body's use of `x` could give its type. No text of the team says how that would be inferred. The chapter that was to say it stayed a heading. Walk runs such a function only because walk checks no types at all. - So the fair summary is: true as a design, half built, and overstated for the last case. ## Nine programs Each program was run on today's tree (`b1e3205e9e`) under walk (`bin/fortress P.fss`) and compiled (`bin/fortress compile P.fss`, then `bin/fortress run P`). A comment marks each place where a type is left out, and gives the line in full. ### 1. The value or the body states the type. Built on both paths. ```fortress component Built export Executable sqr(x: ZZ32) = x x (* left out: the return type. In full: sqr(x: ZZ32): ZZ32 = x x *) apply(f: ZZ32 -> ZZ32, x: ZZ32): ZZ32 = f(x) run(): () = do n = sqr(6) (* left out: the variable's type. In full: n: ZZ32 = sqr(6) *) println n println apply(fn k => k + 1, 41) (* left out: k's type and the result type. In full: fn (k: ZZ32): ZZ32 => k + 1 *) end end ``` - What the words promise: return values and variables without written types. - What is inferred, and from where: the return type of `sqr` from its body; the type of `n` from `sqr(6)`; the type of `k` from the parameter `f: ZZ32 -> ZZ32` of `apply`, which says what kind of function is expected there. - Today: walk prints `36` and `42`. Compiled prints `36` and `42`. This is what Swift and Scala also do for `let n = ...` and for a closure passed to a function. ### 2. The api states the types. Built on both paths. The api, `Shapes.fsi`, states every type once: ```fortress api Shapes object Rect(w: ZZ32, h: ZZ32) tag: String area(): ZZ32 scaled(k: ZZ32): ZZ32 end describe(r: Rect, title: String): String origin: ZZ32 end ``` # Fortress Fortress was Sun Microsystems' experimental programming language for high-performance computation, designed at Sun Labs under **Guy L. Steele Jr.** and **Eric Allen** and developed from 2003 to 2012. The press framed its ambition as doing *"for Fortran what Java did for C"*; the project's own tagline was simpler — **"Simple parallelism, beautiful code."** In practice it became something broader — a laboratory for programming-language ideas that mainstream languages have been absorbing ever since: - **A growable language.** Following Steele's "Growing a Language" (OOPSLA 1998), almost everything — operators, loops, even the parallel machinery behind `∑` — is defined in libraries, not the compiler. - **A mathematical language.** Syntax modeled on whiteboard mathematics: Unicode operators (`∈`, `⊆`, `⌊x⌋`, `∑`), juxtaposition as a user-definable operator (`3 sin pi x`), nontransitive operator precedence (`a+b ∨ c+d` is rejected rather than misparsed), and comments that render as wiki markup. - **A parallel language.** Loops, tuples, argument evaluation, and big reduction operators are implicitly parallel; a work-stealing runtime balances the load ("do for processors what GC does for memory"); `atomic` blocks are backed by transactional memory. - **Traits, multiple inheritance, and symmetric multimethod dispatch**, with overloading checked by the Meet Rule — plus algebraic traits (`Monoid`, `Ring`, …) and design-by-contract woven into the type system. **The revival.** Since August 2026 this repository is being brought back to life: the team's design finished, judged by their own sources, with one program as the measure. [The revival so far](explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/revival-story.md) tells the story for readers outside the project: its purpose, its rule, and where it stands; [the same story as a web page](https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/revival-story/) has the richer presentation. It looked like this — the heart of [`buffons.fss`](ProjectFortress/demos/buffons.fss), one of the original Sun Labs demos, estimating π by Buffon's needle. The `for` loop runs its iterations in parallel, `atomic` guards the shared counters, juxtaposition multiplies, and `0.0 < rsq < 1.0` is a chained comparison: Fortress code was meant to be read as mathematics. The rendering above is the canonical one, produced by [Fortify](Fortify/) — the project's own Emacs-and-LaTeX typesetter, the tool behind the specification and Steele's slides — from the ASCII source you actually type, where `delta_X` is δ_X, `SQRT` is the radical, and `|/ … \|` and `|\ … /|` are ⌈ ⌉ and ⌊ ⌋: ``` for i <- 1#3000 do delta_X = random(2.0) - 1.0 delta_Y = random(2.0) - 1.0 rsq = delta_X^2 + delta_Y^2 if 0.0 < rsq < 1.0 then y1 = tableHeight random(1.0) y2 = y1 + needleLength (delta_Y / SQRT rsq) (y_L, y_H) = (y1 MIN y2, y1 MAX y2) temp1:RR64 = y_L / needleLength temp2:RR64 = y_H / needleLength if |/ temp1 \| = |\ temp2 /| then atomic do hits:= hits + 1.0 end end atomic do n:= n + 1.0 end end end ``` This repository preserves that codebase: the complete surviving history, January 2007 through August 2012, carried forward so that it still builds and runs on today's Java platform. ## History **2003–2006: DARPA HPCS.** Fortress began in 2003 as Sun's language effort within DARPA's High Productivity Computing Systems program, run by Sun Labs' Programming Language Research Group. When DARPA narrowed HPCS funding in late 2006, Sun continued Fortress as a research project. The first public edition of the language specification, [version 1.0α](Specification-history/fortress.1.0alpha.pdf), is dated 19 September 2006. **2007–2008: open source and Fortress 1.0.** The code — at that point the reference interpreter — was opened in January 2007 (this repository's history begins on 4 January 2007). [Version 1.0β](Specification-history/fortress.1.0beta.pdf) of the specification is dated 6 March 2007. The [1.0 specification](Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf), with a matching interpreter release, followed in March 2008. **2008–2012: the type-system frontier.** Work shifted from the interpreter to compiling Fortress to the JVM, and to the hard theory: the Meet Rule, the return type rule, and run-time instantiation of generics. Steele, looking back in 2016, was frank about where that frontier stalled: *"'Non-trivial' is a euphemism for 'exponential cost' […] So we had a grand vision, but could not quite pull it off."* The original repository closes in August 2012 with that problem still open — its last commits record the attempt. **2012: wind-down.** Oracle Labs [concluded the project in the summer of 2012](https://web.archive.org/web/20121007034544/https://blogs.oracle.com/projectfortress/entry/fortress_wrapping_up). **2015–2016: coda.** Steele revisited Fortress in a pair of retrospective talks: [*Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftcIcn8AmSY) at Google (December 2015), on the generator/reducer decomposition at the language's core, and the JuliaCon 2016 keynote [*Fortress Features and Lessons Learned*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EZD3Scuv02g), the fullest account of what the project proved and where it got stuck. ## The research Fortress produced a substantial body of programming-language research. The sources of the specification and of several papers live in this repository. ### The language specification - [`Specification-1.0-frozen/`](Specification-1.0-frozen/) — an unrevised copy of the Working Draft of February 2011; only its [**`fortress.1.0.pdf`**](Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf) is the

\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
\seclabel{revival-changes}
\sloppy

This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
open disagreement.
Each changed passage carries a box headed
``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.

Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
would require.
The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
there.
The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
Fortress~1.0 release.
The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
new one, is in the revival's decision records,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
and, for the number chapters,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
in the same repository.

Each change below follows a decision of the revival.
The first of those decisions, taken on
24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}, is that the compiled type checker keeps
the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
stated, and that the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
satisfy it.
An entry whose change does not follow from route~A says so, and names the
decision it follows or gives its reason.
The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
\secref{revival-routec}.

\subsection{Instantiation exclusion}
\subsection{A string literal as one object}
\seclabel{revival-string-literals}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{literals}; \chapref{objects};
\secref{static-expr}; \secref{revival-object-kinds}.
\item[Change] \secref{literals} says that two string literals of the same text
denote one object, so that every evaluation of a string literal with a given
text yields the same string; that a string that a program builds as it runs is
another object than a literal of the same text, unless the operation that builds
it answers an existing string; and that a concatenation of string literals is a
string literal.
The opening of \chapref{objects} says the same of strict equivalence.
Each passage gains a box, and so does the paragraph of \secref{static-expr} on
the concatenation of literals, which says that it is built.
The effect of \secref{revival-object-kinds} gains a sentence.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 8~November 2026 that two string literals of one text are one object, on both
implementations, and that a concatenation of two string literals is folded into
one literal.
Strings remain reference objects, whose equality of text is their own \EXP{=}
(\secref{revival-object-kinds}).
Every source of the team that speaks of literals makes equal literals one value:
the Working Draft's ``Literals are values; they do not require evaluation''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex}, lines
25--26); the team's restart of 2012, ``All literals represent value objects''
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick},
line 29); and the team's compiled test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_regressions/seqv.fss}, line 22, which
expects \hbox{\rm``\STR{cat}''} to be strictly equivalent to
\hbox{\rm``\STR{cat}''}.
Java, Kotlin, Scala and Clojure, whose strings are Java strings, give equal
literals one object.
The concatenation is the Working Draft's own sentence, which neither of the
team's implementations built.
A reversal would have each evaluation of a string literal construct a new
string, so that two literals of one text are never strictly equivalent, and
would leave a concatenation of literals to be computed when it is evaluated.
The full reasoning is in \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/literals-2026-11-08.md},
sections 6.1 and 6.4, in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] On both implementations
\EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''} \sequiv \hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''}} is \VAR{true}, as
is one literal evaluated twice, and so are
\EXP{(\hbox{\rm``\STR{foo}''} \| \hbox{\rm``\STR{bar}''}) \sequiv \hbox{\rm``\STR{foobar}''}}
and \EXP{(\hbox{\rm``\STR{a}''} \| \hbox{\rm`\STR{b}'}) \sequiv \hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''}},
where the interpreter answered \VAR{false}, and so did the strict equivalence
that the compiled code gives the values of \library\ (row~945 of the revival's
gap ledger); the compiled path's own library answers by text (below).
A string built at run time is not strictly equivalent to an equal literal,
unless the library's operation answers the string it was given, as a substring
that spans its whole string does on both implementations.
The literals of \library\ are strings of this kind too, so that an empty
substring, which \library\ answer with their literal \hbox{\rm``''}, is strictly
equivalent to \hbox{\rm``''}.
The interpreter interns the text of each literal, and compares two flat strings
strictly by the identity of the Java strings that they carry; the compiled code
loads each literal as the Java Virtual Machine's interned string, and its strict
equivalence compares the Java strings that two of its string values carry by
identity.
The concatenation is folded in the desugaring that both implementations run
before the static check.
The compiled path's own library, until \library\ replace it, answers its own
\EXP{\sequiv} on two strings by their text (row~908).
\item[Original text] None: the Working Draft does not say whether two string
literals of the same text are one object.
The passages that this change builds stand, in
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex}, line 57,
``A string literal has type \TYP{String}.'', and in
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/constant.tex}, lines
75--79:
\begin{quote}
The only operation on literals that produces a new literal (as opposed
to a constant) is concatenation by using the operator \EXP{\|}.
One may concatenate mixed string and
character literals, producing a string literal.
For example, ``\txt{foo}''\EXP{\|}''\txt{bar}'' yields ``\txt{foobar}''.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
\seclabel{revival-notrevised}

No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
contradict is known to be unrevised.
The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
(\secref{revival-inference}); the passages that chapter left unrevised, the
sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} by which static parameters were
inferred before the applicability of a declaration was checked and before
declarations were compared, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the
rule of \chapref{overloaded-declarations} on a naked type parameter of bound
\TYP{Any}, are revised with the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading},
\secref{revival-bound}).
The instance of a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter of a declaration that a call
reaches only by dispatch, where nothing fixes it at run time, is not described;
the rule of \secref{resolving-overloading} is for type parameters (row~446 of the
revival's gap ledger).
The sentence of \secref{where-clauses} that a \KWD{where}-clause variable may
not appear as a static argument in an \KWD{extends} clause also refuses a
variable that a constraint fixes to one type; whether it is to be narrowed is
not settled.
The Meet Rule for dotted methods (\secref{more-specific-rule}) asks for a
declaration on the intersection of two parameter types; whether declarations
that together cover the intersection satisfy it too is not settled.
The type of a static call whose argument's static type stands between two
traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses, where its most specific declarations, or a
declaration more specific than them that the call may run, have static
parameters, is not given (\secref{revival-meet}).
Whether two parameter types exclude each other when the only static arguments
at which they could meet are ones that a bound rules out is not settled: the
compiled type checker takes them to exclude where the static argument that the
two parameter types force is a named type that fails the bound, and where a
static parameter that stands at the top of their meet, read as within its
declared bounds, leaves the meet empty, as for row~713's pair, which the
interpreter refuses at load; it reads no bound of a static parameter that
stands inside a static argument (\secref{overloading-static-params}).
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range is
settled (\secref{revival-inference}): it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an
integer numeral does, so the static ranges of \secref{ranges} and the examples
whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds stand as written.
Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
\begin{quote}
The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
library's nested tower today.
They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
behind it.
Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
\seclabel{revival-routec}

The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
instantiations when they form a chain.
The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
type checker and code generator.
Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
types.
Route~C rescues none of the \KWD{where}-clause examples of
\secref{where-clauses} nor the \TYP{Nothing} of \secref{convenience-types},
each of which places one type below infinitely many instantiations, which
no chain contains.
Under route~C the numeric chapters could have kept the nesting of their
widths, and their original text, quoted in \secref{revival-numbers} and the
entries after it and kept in the Working Draft of February 2011, is route~C's
for that nesting; route~C rescues neither the refined number types nor
\TYP{RationalQuantity} (\secref{revival-numbers}).
The record of the experiment is
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md} in the
revival's repository.

## Building, walking and running

Fortress needs only a JDK and Apache Ant; the build has been kept working
on modern JDKs.

```bash
export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=$(pwd)                    # repo root
ant compileAll
./bin/fortress ProjectFortress/demos/buffons.fss
```

That last command *walks* — the interpreter's own term for direct
evaluation — the Buffon's-needle demo excerpted at the top of this README.

There is also a partial JVM bytecode compiler (`fortress compile`, then
`fortress run`); it is incomplete — some constructs were never implemented
— but what exists works. The interpreter requires the filename (without
`.fss`) to match the component name, and the compiler path needs imported
library components compiled into its cache first.

To run the test suite: `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`.

\subsection{The type of a varargs parameter} \seclabel{revival-varargs} \begin{description} \item[Affected sections] \secref{function-decls}. \item[Change] A box after the sentence of \secref{function-decls} that gives a varargs parameter the type \EXP{\TYP{HeapSequence}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} says that no library declares that type, nor the immutable sequence that the team's draft note at the start of \secref{function-app} agreed on in its place; that both implementations give the parameter the array type \EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} of \library; and that the compiled path's own library declares no such type. The normative text is unchanged. \item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the implementers' later word outweighs text that the designers left unfinished. The text and its draft notes name \TYP{HeapSequence} and \TYP{ReadOnlyHeapSequence} (``We agreed to implement varargs tuples using \TYP{ReadOnlyHeapSequence} which is immutable and invariant. We'll add \TYP{MakeReadOnlyHeapSequence} into the core library.''), and no library declares either. The authors of the compiled type checker named a type for the parameter, \EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}, with the comment ``Replace ImmutableArray with ImmutableHeapSequence when ImmutableHeapSequence is put into the libraries'' (\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java}, lines 47--49, in the revival's repository), and the interpreter binds the parameter to an immutable one-dimensional array of the arguments that the factory \VAR{\_\_immutableFactory1} of \library\ builds (\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/NonPrimitive.java}, lines 224--251), a value of that type. The type is immutable, as the draft note asks. Before this change the compiled type checker typed the parameter in the body as \VAR{T}, the type of one argument, and read a parameter list with plain bindings before a varargs binding as if the varargs binding were one more plain binding, so that a call that passed no argument, or more than one, for the varargs binding after plain bindings was refused (row~604 of the revival's gap ledger). The full reasoning is in \nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-defects/REPORT.md} in the revival's repository. \item[Effect] The compiled type checker applies a declaration with a varargs parameter to a call as \secref{function-app} and \secref{applicability-with-special-params} say, whatever the number of arguments for the varargs binding, none among them, each a subtype of the type of the binding or convertible to it; and it types the parameter in the body at \EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} of \library, where it typed it as \VAR{T}. Under the compiled path's own library, which declares no \TYP{ImmutableArray}, it refuses every use of a varargs parameter, in a body, a contract or a function expression, naming the type. The code generator does not yet compile a function with a varargs parameter, so no program with one runs on the compiled path. The interpreter is unchanged. \item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/functions.tex}, lines 178--180, which stand unchanged and are now followed, after the draft note that refers to the library section for \TYP{HeapSequence}, by the box: \begin{quote} The type of a varargs parameter is \EXP{\TYP{HeapSequence}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} where \VAR{T} is the type mentioned in (or inferred for) that binding. \end{quote} \item[Route C] The same under route~C. \end{description} \subsection{The type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out} %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% % Copyright 2009, Oracle and/or its affiliates. % All rights reserved. % % % Use is subject to license terms. % % This distribution may include materials developed by third parties. % %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% \section{Fortress in a Nutshell} \note{Keyword and varargs parameters, components linking, distributions are not yet supported.} Two basic concepts in Fortress are that of \emph{object} and of \emph{trait}.
